  ROI), a shortfall of discrimination rather than calibration. We pursue
  three extensions on the same data: an enlarged feature set screened by
  univariate Plackett–Luce R²; the exploded conditional logit, which fits
  the full finishing order rather than the win alone; and race-level
  interactions through mixed discrete choice. The official rating is the
  strongest new predictor; the exploded fit sharpens coefficient estimates
  without improving win discrimination; and a course-specific draw
  bias—invisible to a pooled draw term because it reverses sign across
  tracks—emerges through the interaction. Backtest ROI improves
  monotonically to `r scales::percent(targets::tar_read(backtest_naive_p2_final)$roi, accuracy = 0.1)`,

  paper 1 is sustained but materially weakened.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Paper 1 replicated the conditional-logit win model of @owen2019 — one of
a line of discrete-choice race models reaching back to @boltonchapman1986
— on UK All-Weather (AW) Flat handicaps and found that the model trails
the betting market across the full threshold range, returning
`r scales::percent(backtest_naive$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` on the §3.4
backtest. We diagnosed the shortfall as a problem of *discrimination*
rather than calibration: a thirteen-feature predictor set is too thin to
compete with a starting price that already aggregates weight, draw,
going, jockey, recent form and informed money. This paper pursues two
remedies — a richer feature set, and a richer use of the race outcome —
on exactly the same data.

We make three contributions, in order. First, an **extended feature
set**, evaluated with an automated univariate screen — a standalone
conditional logit per candidate, ranked by a depth-1 Plackett–Luce $R^2$
against the equal-probability null, following @juola2018. Second, the
**exploded conditional logit**, which treats the full finishing order as
a sequence of conditional win problems and is mathematically equivalent
to maximising the Plackett–Luce likelihood, so the
ranking, not just the win, informs the fit. Third, **race-level
interactions** through the mixed discrete-choice formulation, which
recovers a course-specific draw bias invisible to a win model with a
single pooled draw term. Data scope, race selection and the train/test
split are unchanged from paper 1.

The ROI improves monotonically across the three steps, from
`r scales::percent(backtest_naive$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` in paper 1 to
`r scales::percent(backtest_naive_p2_final$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` in the
final model — but the market continues to dominate. The official rating
(`or_relative`) is the strongest new predictor, and the draw × course
interaction produces the single largest backtest improvement. The
market-efficiency interpretation of paper 1 is sustained, but weakened:
the gap to the starting price narrows substantially without closing.

The paper is organised as follows. @sec-data sets out the data, the
two-tier feature set and the three data decisions specific to this paper.
@sec-eda evaluates every candidate feature through the univariate screen
and records the feature drop and keep decisions. @sec-extended-win fits
the extended win model and contrasts it with paper 1 and Owen's Table 3.
@sec-exploded-logit refits via the exploded logit and asks whether the
ranking sharpens prediction. @sec-mixed-interactions tests the two
race-level interactions and selects the final model. @sec-discussion
draws the threads together and signposts paper 3, and
@sec-appx-derivations derives the Plackett–Luce and mixed-choice
machinery in full.
